When using Netlify to publish a React app, you would typically use a serverless function, such as AWS Lambda, to handle the connection to the database. This function can be triggered by an HTTP request from your React app, allowing you to retrieve or update data in the database.

  3. Use the function to handle database queries and operations, such as fetching or updating data.
  4. In your React app, use fetch or axios to make an HTTP request to the AWS Lambda function, passing any necessary parameters in the request.
  5. Use the data returned from the function to update the state of your React components.

It is important to keep in mind that this is just one way of connecting to a database when using Netlify, and there are many other options like using a cloud database provider like AWS RDS, MongoDB Atlas, Firebase etc.
What databases work well with React?

There are many different databases that can be used with React, some popular options include:

  1. MongoDB: A document-based NoSQL database that is commonly used with the Mongoose library to interact with MongoDB from Node.js.

  2. Firebase: A cloud-based platform that provides a real-time database and authentication services. It also provides SDKs for different languages including React

  3. MySQL: A popular open-source relational database that can be used with the MySQL library for Node.js.

  4. PostgreSQL: Another popular open-source relational database that can be used with the pg library for Node.js.

  5. AWS RDS: A fully managed relational database service provided by Amazon Web Services, which supports multiple database engines including MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server.

Ultimately, the best database for your React app will depend on your specific requirements and the type of data you need to store. NoSQL databases like MongoDB and Firebase are well suited for handling large amounts of unstructured data, while relational databases like MySQL and PostgreSQL are better suited for structured data.
What do you mean by structured and unstructured data? Do you mean nomralised?

Yes, structured data refers to data that is organized in a specific way, often using a relational model, and follows a specific schema. For example, data stored in a table with rows and columns in a relational database like MySQL or PostgreSQL is considered structured data. Structured data is often normalized, meaning that it is split into multiple tables to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity.

On the other hand, unstructured data refers to data that does not have a specific format or organization. It can be free-form text, images, videos, audio files, etc. Unstructured data is often stored in a NoSQL database like MongoDB or Firebase, which allows for more flexible and dynamic data storage. Since unstructured data doesn't follow any specific schema, it can be stored in the form of a document, key-value pairs, or even graph databases.

It is worth noting that today with the use of powerful tools and technologies, unstructured data can be transformed and made searchable, and structured data can be stored in NoSQL databases.

Here is a detailed walkthrough:

  1. Set up the project:

Create a new Spring Boot project with the Web and Reactive dependencies. You can do this by going to https://start.spring.io/ and selecting the following options:

  • Project: Maven Project
  • Language: Java
  • Packaging: Jar

Once the project is generated, import it into your favorite IDE.

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import reactor.bus.EventBus;

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
import reactor.bus.Event;

@RestController
public class MyController {

    @Autowired
    private EventBus eventBus;

    @PostMapping("/triggerEvent")
    public String triggerEvent(@RequestParam("message") String message) {
        eventBus.notify("eventHandlerKey", Event.wrap(message));
        return "Event triggered!";
    }
}

Create a simple event handler class that will process the events:

import reactor.bus.Event;
import reactor.fn.Consumer;

public class MyEventHandler implements Consumer<Event<String>> {

    @Override
    public void accept(Event<String> event) {
        String message = event.getData();
        System.out.println("Received message: " + message);
    }
}

Update the AppConfig class to register the event handler:

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import reactor.bus.EventBus;

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public EventBus eventBus() {
        EventBus eventBus = EventBus.create();
        eventBus.on("eventHandlerKey", new MyEventHandler());
        return eventBus;
    }
}
